title: Traditions: prize giving, teams and customs
summary: How the ceremonies and the prize giving work, how teams compete, and the customs that turn a Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting competition into a celebration.

body.html: A competition is more than a score. Shooters keep customs that turn a long day into a shared celebration: the ceremonies, the prize giving, team spirit and small courtesies on the ground.

If two or more shooters have the same score for one of the top three places, a shoot-off decides it: they shoot extra targets, and the better score wins. It is often the most exciting moment of the day, and spectators gather round. How shoot-offs and other ties work: Categories, classes and shoot-offs.

Team events are a tradition of their own. A team is a few shooters from one country, or from one club at club events. Their scores are added up for the team ranking. Teams do not shoot a shoot-off. If two teams finish level, the team whose shooters scored more together on the last round of the competition wins. If that is level too, the round before decides, and so on.

International events open and close with a ceremony. At the opening, national teams parade in their team outfit or in smart trousers and a blazer. At the closing, all prize winners must attend the prize giving, dressed the same way.
This ceremony rule is the same in both disciplines. Club events are usually less formal, so read the programme. The dress code on the stand is a separate rule: Dress code and safety on the stand.
Stepping onto the podium is also a mark of respect: for the rivals who shot alongside you and for the people who ran the event.

There are informal customs too: congratulating the winner, a photo of your squad (the group you shot with), a thank-you to the organisers, the referees and the trappers. Manners on the stand itself: Sportsmanship and manners in the squad.

key_points.html: At international events all prize winners must attend the prize giving.
Ceremony dress: team outfit, or smart trousers and a blazer.
Team scores are added up; teams do not shoot a shoot-off.
At the end of the day, thank the organisers, the referees and the trappers.

did_you_know.html: In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™, organisers of international events try to put team-mates from one country into different squads (shooting groups). So at a big championship you often shoot alongside people from other nations.

quiz.q: What must prize winners do at an international event?

options.text: Send a team-mate to collect the prize
Attend the prize giving, properly dressed
Wear their shooting vest on the podium

quiz.explain: All prize winners attend the closing ceremony in team outfit, or in smart trousers and a blazer.

options.text: By their scores on the last rounds
By a shoot-off between the teams
By drawing lots after the event

quiz.explain: Teams do not shoot off. The last round of the competition decides (in Sporting™ the 8th layout, in Compak® Sporting the 8th field); if that is level too, the one before, and so on.

quiz.q: Who do shooters usually thank at the end of the day?

options.text: Only the winner of the event
Only the coach who came with them

quiz.explain: A competition runs on many people's work, and a short thank-you is a common custom.
